title: The Green Sahara dries out
summary: As the African Humid Period ends, the Sahara's lakes and grasslands turn to desert, pushing herders toward the Nile valley and the Sahel.
description: During the African Humid Period, roughly 14,500 to 5,000 years ago, a stronger West African monsoon driven by changes in Earth's orbit watered the Sahara, supporting lakes, grasslands, hippos and cattle herders whose lives are recorded in rock art from Tassili n'Ajjer to the Gilf Kebir. As summer sunlight in the Northern Hemisphere weakened, rainfall declined and the region became desert, with most of the change complete by about 3000–2500 BCE. The drying pushed people toward reliable water, and many archaeologists link it to population growth along the Nile on the eve of Egyptian state formation and to the spread of pastoralism into the Sahel and East Africa. Whether the end was abrupt across the whole region or staggered from place to place remains debated: marine dust records suggest a rapid shift, while lake records point to a more gradual, regionally variable one.

title: Uruk, the first great city
summary: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grows into perhaps the world's largest city, with monumental temples, mass-produced ration bowls and a temple bureaucracy.
description: During the Late Uruk period the settlement of Uruk, on a branch of the Euphrates in what is now southern Iraq, expanded to around 250 hectares and perhaps 25,000–50,000 inhabitants, making it arguably the first true city. Its Eanna and Anu precincts held massive mudbrick temples decorated with clay-cone mosaics, and standardised bevelled-rim bowls suggest rations issued by a central institution. Uruk-style colonies and outposts appeared as far away as Habuba Kabira in Syria and Godin Tepe in Iran, in what archaeologists call the Uruk expansion. The administrative needs of this society produced cylinder seals, numerical tablets and, ultimately, writing. Population estimates and the nature of the expansion, whether trade, colonisation or something else, are still debated.

title: Writing is invented in Mesopotamia
summary: Scribes at Uruk begin recording goods and labour on clay tablets, among the earliest known writing anywhere and the ancestor of cuneiform.
description: The earliest proto-cuneiform tablets, found mainly in the Eanna precinct of Uruk, record rations, livestock, land and workers using pictographic signs and numerical notation; they date to roughly 3400–3200 BCE. Writing seems to have grown out of older accounting tools such as clay tokens, sealed clay envelopes and purely numerical tablets. Over the following centuries the signs became wedge-shaped impressions made with a reed stylus and began to record the sounds of the Sumerian language, making it possible to write names, laws, letters and literature. Cuneiform was later adapted for Akkadian, Hittite, Elamite and other languages and remained in use for more than 3,000 years, until about the 1st century CE. Egyptian hieroglyphs appeared at about the same time, and whether the two inventions were independent is still discussed.

title: Liangzhu: walled city and dams of the Yangtze delta
summary: Rice farmers of the lower Yangtze build a walled city of about 300 hectares, great earthen dams and jade workshops, one of East Asia's earliest states.
description: The Liangzhu culture flourished around Lake Tai in the lower Yangtze delta from about 3300 to 2300 BCE. Its centre near modern Hangzhou was a walled city of about 300 hectares built on wetlands, with a raised palace platform, elite cemeteries and an outer ring of settlements. To the north and west, a system of eleven earthen dams and embankments, built around 3100–2700 BCE and among the earliest large-scale water-control works known anywhere, managed floods and water transport, while intensive rice farming fed the population. Elite graves contain finely carved jade cong tubes and bi discs, often bearing a shared mask motif that suggests common religious beliefs. Many archaeologists regard Liangzhu as an early state, and it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019; its decline around 2300 BCE may be linked to severe flooding.

title: Earliest Egyptian hieroglyphs at Abydos
summary: Small bone and ivory labels from tomb U-j at Abydos carry some of the oldest known Egyptian hieroglyphic signs.
description: Excavations at Umm el-Qa'ab, the royal cemetery of Abydos in Upper Egypt, uncovered tomb U-j, the burial of a late Predynastic ruler, containing around 200 small inscribed labels along with ink-painted jars. Many specialists read the signs as early hieroglyphs recording place-names or commodities with phonetic values, which would make them roughly contemporary with, or slightly older than, the first Mesopotamian tablets. Hieroglyphic writing developed rapidly over the following centuries for royal names, monuments and administration, while cursive hieratic was used for everyday documents. Whether Egyptian writing was invented independently or stimulated by contact with Mesopotamia is debated, though the two systems differ markedly. The script was used until the late 4th century CE and was deciphered by Jean-François Champollion in 1822.

title: One of the world's oldest wooden wheels
summary: A wooden wheel and axle preserved in the Ljubljana Marshes of Slovenia show that wheeled carts were in use in Copper Age Europe.
description: The Ljubljana Marshes Wheel, found in 2002 at a waterlogged pile-dwelling site in Slovenia, is a solid disc of ash wood about 70 cm across, discovered with an oak axle; radiocarbon dating places it around 3150 BCE. Wheeled vehicles appear almost simultaneously across a wide region from Mesopotamia to the Pontic–Caspian steppe and central Europe between about 3500 and 3300 BCE, shown by pictograms at Uruk, the wagon image on the Bronocice pot in Poland, and clay models. Where the wheel-and-axle was first invented is unknown, and its rapid spread suggests the idea travelled quickly once devised. Early wheels were heavy and solid; light spoked wheels for chariots came more than a thousand years later.

title: Mythical start date of the Long Count calendar
summary: The Mesoamerican Long Count counts days from a creation date equivalent to 11 August 3114 BCE, though the calendar itself was devised much later.
description: The Long Count, used by the Maya and their neighbours, counts elapsed days in units of k'in, winal, tun, k'atun and b'ak'tun from a mythical base date written 13.0.0.0.0 4 Ajaw 8 Kumk'u. Under the widely accepted Goodman–Martínez–Thompson correlation this corresponds to 11 August 3114 BCE in the proleptic Gregorian calendar (6 September in the Julian). No known event happened then; Maya texts treat it as the beginning of the present world, while the system itself is first attested on monuments of the 1st century BCE, such as Stela 2 at Chiapa de Corzo and Stela C at Tres Zapotes. The completion of the 13th b'ak'tun on 21 December 2012 prompted widespread but unfounded predictions of catastrophe.

title: Narmer and the unification of Egypt
summary: Egypt becomes a single kingdom along the Nile under the First Dynasty, traditionally founded by Menes, usually identified with Narmer.
description: By around 3100 BCE the rival polities of Upper (southern) Egypt and the Nile Delta had been joined into one state ruled by a single king, beginning the First Dynasty. The Narmer Palette from Hierakonpolis shows a king wearing the white crown of the south on one side and the red crown of the north on the other, and Narmer is usually identified with Menes, the unifier named in later king lists and credited with founding Memphis. Unification was probably a gradual process spanning several generations of 'Dynasty 0' rulers rather than a single conquest. Radiocarbon studies suggest the First Dynasty began between about 3200 and 3000 BCE. The result was the world's first large territorial state, whose kingship, administration and writing set patterns that endured for some 3,000 years.

title: Stonehenge is built
dateLabel: c. 3000–1600 BCE; sarsen circle c. 2500 BCE
summary: On Salisbury Plain, Neolithic Britons build Stonehenge in stages, raising its great sarsen circle, aligned on the solstices, around 2500 BCE.
description: Stonehenge began around 3000 BCE as a circular ditch and bank enclosing cremation burials. Around 2500 BCE the builders raised the sarsen circle and inner horseshoe of trilithons, using sandstone blocks of up to about 30 tonnes, most of them sourced at West Woods some 25 km to the north, while the smaller bluestones were brought about 225 km from the Preseli Hills in Wales and the Altar Stone, research in 2024 showed, from north-east Scotland. The monument is aligned on the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset, and nearby Durrington Walls may have housed the people who built it or gathered there for feasts. The stones were rearranged several times until about 1600 BCE. Its precise purpose, whether ceremonial site, burial ground, calendar marker or all of these, remains debated.

title: Caral and the first civilization of the Americas
summary: In Peru's Supe Valley, the Caral–Supe (Norte Chico) people build platform mounds and sunken plazas, without pottery and with little sign of warfare.
description: The Caral–Supe or Norte Chico civilization arose in a cluster of river valleys on the arid central coast of Peru, where more than 30 sites with monumental architecture have been identified. Its best-known centre, Caral, covers over 60 hectares with six large platform mounds and circular sunken plazas, built mostly between about 2600 and 2000 BCE, while radiocarbon dates from nearby sites reach back to around 3000 BCE or earlier. The economy combined irrigated cotton, squash and beans inland with intensive fishing for anchovies on the coast. The culture made no ceramics, and evidence of large-scale warfare is scarce. A knotted string found at Caral has been interpreted as a possible early quipu, though this is uncertain. It is the oldest known complex society in the Americas, roughly contemporary with the Egyptian pyramids.

title: Rival city-states of Sumer
summary: Ur, Lagash, Umma, Kish and other Sumerian cities, each with its own patron god and ruler, compete for land and water in southern Mesopotamia.
description: In the Early Dynastic period southern Mesopotamia was divided among a dozen or more independent city-states, each centred on the temple of a patron deity and led by a ruler titled en, ensi or lugal. Their rivalries are recorded in some of the first historical inscriptions, such as the Stele of the Vultures, which celebrates Lagash's victory over neighbouring Umma in a long dispute over irrigated border land. The Royal Cemetery at Ur, excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s, revealed tombs of about 2600 BCE filled with gold, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan and sacrificed attendants. Writing expanded during this period from accounting to royal inscriptions, letters and early literature.

title: Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara
summary: Egypt's first pyramid, a six-stepped tomb for King Djoser traditionally credited to Imhotep, is the earliest colossal cut-stone building known.
description: Built during the Third Dynasty for King Djoser, the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the necropolis of Memphis, began as a square stone mastaba tomb that was enlarged several times into six stacked tiers about 62 m high. It stood at the centre of a vast walled complex of courts, shrines and dummy buildings that reproduce in limestone forms previously built in mudbrick, timber and reed. Later Egyptian tradition credited its design to Djoser's official Imhotep, whose name and titles appear on a statue base found at the site and who was eventually revered as a god of wisdom and medicine. Beneath the pyramid lies a maze of shafts and galleries, some lined with blue faience tiles. The monument opened the age of pyramid building that culminated about a century later at Giza; Djoser's reign is usually dated to around 2670–2650 BCE, though estimates vary by several decades.

title: Cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation
summary: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and other planned cities with grid streets, covered drains and standard weights flourish across today's Pakistan and northwest India.
description: The Mature Harappan phase of the Indus Valley Civilisation spanned an area larger than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, from Balochistan to Gujarat and the upper Ganges plain. Cities such as Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were laid out with orderly streets, brick houses with bathrooms, covered drains and large public structures such as the Great Bath, while uniform bricks and stone weights point to strong shared standards. Indus seals carrying a short, still-undeciphered script have been found as far away as Mesopotamia, whose texts refer to trade with a land called Meluhha. Unusually, no clear palaces, royal tombs or monumental images of rulers have been found, and how the society was governed remains unknown. From about 1900 BCE the cities were gradually abandoned, probably owing to a combination of shifting rivers, weakening monsoons and changes in trade.

title: Great Pyramid of Giza
summary: Pharaoh Khufu's pyramid at Giza, about 146 m tall, is completed; it remained the tallest human-made structure for more than 3,800 years.
description: Built for the Fourth Dynasty king Khufu over roughly two decades, the Great Pyramid originally stood about 146.6 m high and contains some 2.3 million blocks of limestone and granite, with its sides aligned to the cardinal directions to within a fraction of a degree. It crowned an architectural sequence that began with Djoser's Step Pyramid at Saqqara and continued through Sneferu's pyramids at Meidum and Dahshur. Khufu's successors Khafre and Menkaure added two further pyramids at Giza, and the Great Sphinx was carved, probably under Khafre. Excavations of the workers' town and cemeteries nearby, and the papyri of the official Merer, show that the pyramids were built by organised crews of fed and housed Egyptian labourers, not slaves. It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still largely intact.

title: Pyramids built by aliens or Atlanteans (fringe claim)
dateLabel: c. 2560 BCE (conventional date of the Great Pyramid)
summary: Ancient-astronaut and lost-civilisation writers claim the Giza pyramids were built with alien help or by survivors of Atlantis.
description: Since the late 1960s, writers such as Erich von Däniken have argued that ancient monuments, including the Giza pyramids, were too sophisticated for their builders and must reflect help from extraterrestrial visitors. A related strand, going back to Ignatius Donnelly's Atlantis (1882) and the psychic Edgar Cayce, attributes the pyramids or a hidden 'Hall of Records' to refugees from a lost advanced civilisation, and Robert Bauval's Orion correlation theory proposes that the three Giza pyramids encode a sky pattern of about 10,500 BCE. These ideas remain popular in books and television documentaries. Proponents differ on dates, some accepting the conventional Old Kingdom chronology and others pushing the monuments back thousands of years; this entry is placed at the conventional date of the Great Pyramid.
mainstreamView: Egyptologists can trace how the pyramids were built: a clear developmental sequence from mastaba tombs through Djoser's Step Pyramid and Sneferu's experimental pyramids, quarries with tool marks and abandoned blocks, construction ramps, the excavated workers' town at Heit el-Ghurab with its bakeries and cemeteries, and the Wadi al-Jarf papyri recording the shipment of limestone for Khufu's pyramid. Radiocarbon dates from organic material in the mortar fall in the 3rd millennium BCE, and there is no physical evidence of extraterrestrial technology or of Atlantis, which Plato presented as a philosophical allegory. Critics also point out that such claims deny ancient Egyptians credit for their own achievements.

title: Sphinx water-erosion hypothesis (fringe claim)
dateLabel: claimed c. 7000–5000 BCE or earlier; conventionally c. 2500 BCE
summary: Some authors argue that weathering on the Great Sphinx's enclosure was caused by heavy rainfall, making the monument thousands of years older than Khafre.
description: The author John Anthony West set out the idea in his 1979 book Serpent in the Sky, building on remarks by the esoteric writer R. A. Schwaller de Lubicz, and in the early 1990s the Boston University geologist Robert Schoch took it up. They argued that deep vertical fissures and rounded profiles in the limestone walls of the Sphinx enclosure were cut by prolonged rainfall runoff, which would require the wetter climate of the period before about 3000 BCE. Schoch suggested the core body of the Sphinx dates to around 7000–5000 BCE, while others, including West and Graham Hancock, have proposed 10,500 BCE or earlier and linked it to a lost civilisation. The idea received wide attention through a 1993 television documentary. The entry is shown at the conventional date of the Sphinx, about 2500 BCE.
mainstreamView: Most geologists and Egyptologists attribute the weathering to processes acting on soft, unevenly layered limestone over some 4,500 years, including salt crystallisation, wind erosion and occasional heavy rains in historical times. Quarry evidence shows that the Sphinx was carved from the same rock as the blocks used in the adjacent Sphinx and valley temples of Khafre, and no tools, settlements or other traces of a sophisticated culture from 7000–10,500 BCE have been found at Giza, where the earliest substantial occupation matches the Old Kingdom.

title: Kerma, the first kingdom of Kush
summary: At Kerma near the Nile's Third Cataract, a Nubian kingdom grows rich on trade in gold, ivory and ebony and comes to rival Middle Kingdom Egypt.
description: Kerma, in what is now northern Sudan, developed from around 2500 BCE into the capital of a powerful Nubian state, known to the Egyptians as Kush. Its huge mudbrick temple, the Western Deffufa, still stands, and royal burials under giant tumuli contained hundreds of sacrificed people and animals. Kerma controlled trade routes bringing gold, ivory, ebony and incense from the south, and at its height around 1650–1550 BCE its armies raided deep into southern Egypt, possibly in alliance with the Hyksos. Egypt's New Kingdom pharaohs conquered Kerma around 1500 BCE, but Kushite culture endured and later gave rise to the kingdom of Napata.

title: The Bantu expansion begins
summary: Bantu-speaking farmers begin spreading from the Nigeria–Cameroon borderlands, eventually carrying their languages across most of sub-Saharan Africa.
description: The several hundred Bantu languages spoken today across central, eastern and southern Africa descend from a common ancestor spoken in the region of the Cameroon Grassfields and eastern Nigeria. Linguistic, archaeological and genetic evidence indicates that Bantu-speaking communities began moving out of this homeland roughly 4,000–5,000 years ago, first southward through or around the equatorial rainforest and later eastward to the Great Lakes, bringing farming, pottery and, in later phases, ironworking. Over the next three millennia they reached as far as South Africa, absorbing or displacing many hunter-gatherer populations. The routes and timing are debated: some studies favour an early movement south through the rainforest followed by expansion east, while others emphasise a route along its northern edge. It was one of the largest population movements in human history.

title: Sargon of Akkad founds the Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian city-states and rules from the Persian Gulf to Syria, in what is often called the world's first empire.
description: Sargon, a man of obscure origins who rose to power at Kish, conquered the cities of Sumer and campaigned up the Euphrates to Mari, Ebla and the 'Cedar Forest' of Lebanon, uniting Mesopotamia under the dynasty of Akkad. His capital, Akkad (Agade), has never been located but probably lay in central Iraq. Akkadian, a Semitic language, became the language of administration, his daughter Enheduanna served as high priestess at Ur and is the earliest author known by name, and his grandson Naram-Sin declared himself a god and 'king of the four quarters'. The empire collapsed around 2154 BCE amid revolts and incursions by the Gutians, possibly worsened by the 4.2-kiloyear drought. Its dates depend on which Mesopotamian chronology is used and may be off by several decades.

title: The 4.2-kiloyear drought
summary: A centuries-long arid phase from about 2200 BCE coincides with crises in Akkad, Egypt, the Indus and China, and marks the start of the Meghalayan Age.
description: Lake sediments, cave stalagmites and marine cores from the Mediterranean to India and China record a pronounced dry and in places cool phase beginning around 4,200 years ago. A stalagmite from Mawmluh Cave in Meghalaya, India, was chosen as the reference for the start of the Meghalayan Age, the latest stage of the Holocene, formally ratified in 2018. Many researchers link the drought to the abandonment of northern Mesopotamian cities such as Tell Leilan, the fall of the Akkadian Empire, low Nile floods during Egypt's First Intermediate Period, and the decline of Indus and Neolithic Chinese cultures. Others argue that the climate signal was not globally synchronous and that political and social causes mattered more.
mainstreamView: A significant climatic anomaly around 4,200 years ago is well documented in many records, especially in the Middle East and South Asia, and it formally defines the Meghalayan Age. Whether it was a truly global, simultaneous event, and how far it caused rather than merely coincided with the collapse of states, remains actively debated.

title: Ur III: the Ziggurat of Ur and Ur-Nammu's law code
summary: Ur-Nammu reunites Sumer under the Third Dynasty of Ur, whose kings build the great ziggurat and issue the oldest law code known to survive.
description: After the fall of Akkad and a period of Gutian dominance, Ur-Nammu of Ur took control of southern Mesopotamia around 2112 BCE and founded the Third Dynasty of Ur, often called Ur III. He began the great stepped temple tower, or ziggurat, of the moon god Nanna at Ur, whose massive mudbrick core still stands, its lower stages partly reconstructed in the 20th century. The Code of Ur-Nammu, attributed to him or to his son Shulgi, is the oldest law code known to survive, some three centuries older than Hammurabi's, and it set compensation in silver for many injuries. Under Shulgi the state built up a vast bureaucracy whose tens of thousands of clay tablets record taxes, rations and labour in great detail, and Sumerian literature flourished at court. The dynasty fell around 2004 BCE, when Elamites sacked Ur, an event later mourned in the Lament for Ur.

title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
dateLabel: Sumerian poems c. 2100 BCE; Akkadian epic c. 1800 BCE
summary: Poems about Gilgamesh, a king of Uruk, are written down in Sumerian and later woven into the first great epic of world literature.
description: Gilgamesh was probably a historical king of Uruk in the early 3rd millennium BCE who became a hero of legend. Five separate Sumerian poems about him are known from copies of the Ur III and Old Babylonian periods, and by about 1800 BCE they had been combined into an Akkadian epic about friendship, death and the search for immortality. The best-known version, the Standard Babylonian epic of twelve tablets attributed to the scholar Sîn-lēqi-unninni, was found in the 7th-century BCE library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. Its flood story, told by Utnapishtim, closely parallels the biblical account of Noah, a resemblance that caused a sensation when George Smith announced it in 1872.

title: Xia dynasty and the Erlitou culture
summary: Chinese tradition names the Xia as the first dynasty; many archaeologists link it to the palatial site of Erlitou, but no Xia writing has been found.
description: Later Chinese histories such as Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian describe the Xia as China's first dynasty, founded by Yu the Great after he tamed catastrophic floods, with seventeen kings before its overthrow by the Shang. The government-sponsored Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project dated it to about 2070–1600 BCE. The Erlitou culture of the Yellow River valley in Henan, about 1900–1500 BCE, had palace foundations, roads, workshops producing the earliest Chinese bronze ritual vessels, and turquoise-inlaid objects, making it the leading candidate for a Xia capital. However, no contemporary inscriptions name the Xia.
mainstreamView: Many Chinese archaeologists identify Erlitou with the later Xia, while many Western scholars regard the Xia as unproven, since the earliest written references date from the Zhou period, roughly a thousand years later. Erlitou itself is generally accepted as an early state-level society; the debate is over whether it can be given the traditional dynastic name.

title: Spoke-wheeled chariots appear on the steppe
summary: Warrior elites of the Sintashta culture in the southern Urals are buried with the earliest known chariots, light two-wheeled vehicles with spoked wheels.
description: Graves of the Sintashta culture, which flourished east of the southern Ural Mountains from about 2100 to 1800 BCE, contain the oldest known spoke-wheeled chariots, often buried with pairs of horses, bone cheekpieces for controlling them, and weapons. Sintashta communities lived in fortified settlements such as Sintashta and Arkaim and worked copper and bronze on a large scale. Lighter spoked wheels made a fast horse-drawn vehicle possible, and chariot warfare spread within a few centuries to the Near East, Egypt and India, reaching Shang China by about 1200 BCE. Ancient DNA shows that a lineage of domestic horses from the western Eurasian steppe expanded across Eurasia from about 2200 BCE, around the time the chariot appeared, and many scholars link Sintashta to the ancestors of Indo-Iranian-speaking peoples. Some researchers argue that the earliest steppe vehicles were too small for warfare and served for racing or ritual, and whether the chariot was first developed on the steppe or in the Near East is still discussed.

title: Minoan palaces of Crete
summary: Knossos, Phaistos and Malia rise as great palace complexes, centres of a seafaring Bronze Age civilization on Crete.
description: The Minoan civilization, named by Arthur Evans after the legendary King Minos, developed on Crete from about 3000 BCE and built its first palaces around 1900 BCE. Knossos, the largest, was a multi-storey complex of courtyards, storerooms, light wells and vivid frescoes showing bull-leaping, processions and marine life. Minoan traders reached Egypt, the Levant and the Aegean islands, and administrators used the undeciphered Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A scripts. After earthquake damage the palaces were rebuilt around 1700 BCE, but most were destroyed around 1450 BCE, after which Knossos came under Mycenaean Greek control, as shown by tablets in Linear B.

title: Code of Hammurabi
summary: Hammurabi of Babylon has 282 laws carved on a black stone stele, one of the longest and best-preserved law codes of the ancient world.
description: Hammurabi, who ruled Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE, turned a modest city-state into the dominant power of Mesopotamia by defeating Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. Late in his reign he issued a set of laws, best known from a 2.25 m stone stele now in the Louvre, which had been carried off to Susa as war booty and was rediscovered there in 1901. Its prologue presents the king as appointed by the gods to bring justice, and its rulings cover trade, wages, family law and injury, with punishments that often varied by social class and include the principle of 'an eye for an eye'. It was not the first law code, following those of Ur-Nammu and Lipit-Ishtar, and scholars debate whether it was applied in courts or served mainly as a royal statement of justice. Exact dates depend on which Mesopotamian chronology is used.

title: Poverty Point earthworks
summary: Hunter-gatherers in the lower Mississippi Valley build giant concentric earthen ridges and mounds at Poverty Point, Louisiana.
description: Poverty Point, in northeastern Louisiana, consists of six concentric C-shaped earthen ridges about 1.2 km across, together with several large mounds, the biggest over 20 m high. It was built by people who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering rather than farming, making it one of the largest earthwork complexes ever created by a non-agricultural society. Research suggests that parts of the site, including its largest mound, were raised very quickly, possibly within a few months. Copper from the Great Lakes, galena from Missouri and stone from the Appalachians show that it was the hub of a far-reaching exchange network. It was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.

title: The Hittite kingdom rises in Anatolia
summary: From their capital Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittites build a great power that sacks Babylon and rivals Egypt for control of Syria.
description: The Hittites, speakers of the earliest well-attested Indo-European language, founded a kingdom in central Anatolia around 1650 BCE under Hattusili I, with its capital at Hattusa near modern Boğazkale, Turkey. His successor Mursili I raided far down the Euphrates and sacked Babylon around 1595 BCE (middle chronology), ending Hammurabi's dynasty. In the 14th century BCE Suppiluliuma I made the Hittite state one of the great powers of the Near East, dominating northern Syria. The empire collapsed around 1180 BCE in the wider Late Bronze Age crisis, and Hattusa was abandoned. The Hittites were largely forgotten until archives of cuneiform tablets were excavated at Hattusa from 1906 and their language was deciphered by Bedřich Hrozný in 1915.

title: The Thera (Minoan) eruption
summary: A colossal eruption of the Santorini volcano buries the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri in ash and sends tsunamis across the Aegean.
description: The eruption of Thera (Santorini), estimated at VEI 6 or 7 and one of the largest volcanic events of the past 10,000 years, blew out much of the island and enlarged its flooded caldera. The town of Akrotiri was buried under metres of pumice and ash, preserving multi-storey buildings and wall paintings, though its inhabitants seem to have evacuated in time. Tsunami deposits have been found on Crete and in western Turkey, and the eruption may have weakened Minoan civilization, although the Cretan palaces continued for several generations afterwards. Its date has long been disputed: radiocarbon dating, including an olive branch buried by the pumice, points to about 1630–1600 BCE, while traditional links with Egyptian archaeology suggest about 1550–1500 BCE, and recent tree-ring calibrations have narrowed but not closed the gap.
mainstreamView: That a huge eruption destroyed Akrotiri early in the Late Minoan IA period is undisputed. Most scientists favour a late 17th- or early 16th-century BCE date based on radiocarbon, while some archaeologists still prefer a date around 1500 BCE based on Egyptian and Aegean pottery chronologies; the eruption is also sometimes linked, speculatively, to the Atlantis legend.

title: Mycenaean Greece
summary: Warrior elites at Mycenae, Pylos and Thebes build fortified palaces and keep records in Linear B, the earliest written Greek.
description: Mainland Greek culture was transformed from about 1600 BCE, when the rich shaft graves at Mycenae, with their gold masks and weapons, signal the rise of a warrior aristocracy. By the 14th and 13th centuries BCE palace centres such as Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos and Thebes had massive 'Cyclopean' walls, beehive tombs like the Treasury of Atreus, and bureaucracies that recorded goods and personnel on clay tablets in Linear B. Michael Ventris's decipherment of Linear B in 1952 showed that its language is an early form of Greek. The Mycenaeans took over Knossos around 1450 BCE and traded across the Mediterranean. Most of their palaces were destroyed around 1200 BCE, and many later Greek myths, including the Trojan War, are thought to preserve distorted memories of this age.

title: The Shang dynasty
summary: Shang kings rule the Yellow River plain, casting monumental bronzes and leaving the earliest known Chinese writing.
description: The Shang is the earliest Chinese dynasty confirmed by contemporary written records. Its early capitals included the walled city at Zhengzhou, and from about 1250 BCE the kings ruled from Yin, near modern Anyang, where excavations since 1928 have uncovered palaces, royal tombs and workshops. Shang society was headed by a king who acted as chief priest to the royal ancestors, and its elites used chariots, practised human sacrifice and cast ritual vessels in bronze with remarkable skill. The dynasty was overthrown by the Zhou around 1046 BCE. Its traditional starting date of about 1600 BCE comes from later histories and the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project and remains approximate.

title: Egypt's New Kingdom
summary: After expelling the Hyksos, Theban pharaohs build an empire from Syria to Nubia and fill Thebes and the Valley of the Kings with temples and tombs.
description: Ahmose I founded the Eighteenth Dynasty around 1550 BCE by driving out the Hyksos, rulers of Levantine origin who had controlled the Nile Delta during the Second Intermediate Period. His successors, notably Thutmose I and Thutmose III, campaigned as far as the Euphrates and conquered Nubia down to the Fourth Cataract, making Egypt an imperial power. Wealth from tribute and Nubian gold mines funded the vast temple complex of Karnak, Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari, and royal tombs cut into the Valley of the Kings, including that of Tutankhamun. The Ramesside kings of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Dynasties kept Egypt among the great powers until the period ended around 1070 BCE with the country divided.

title: Velikovsky's Worlds in Collision (fringe claim)
summary: Immanuel Velikovsky claimed that a comet ejected from Jupiter, later the planet Venus, passed close to Earth around 1500 BCE, causing the plagues of the Exodus.
description: In his bestselling Worlds in Collision (1950), the psychiatrist Immanuel Velikovsky argued that myths and ancient texts from many cultures preserve eyewitness accounts of real cosmic catastrophes. In his scenario a comet-like body expelled from Jupiter passed Earth around the 15th century BCE, raining fire and stones, briefly halting Earth's rotation and producing the plagues and the parting of the sea described in Exodus, before settling into orbit as the planet Venus; Mars then supposedly made close approaches in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE. In later books such as Ages in Chaos he proposed shortening Egyptian chronology by several centuries to fit his theory. The book's reception, including a campaign by some scientists against its publisher, became a celebrated controversy.
mainstreamView: Astronomers reject the scenario because it violates celestial mechanics and the conservation of energy and angular momentum; Venus is a rocky planet about 4.5 billion years old, not a recent body ejected from a gas giant. Ice cores, tree rings, ocean sediments and other records show no global catastrophe or interruption of Earth's rotation in the 2nd or 1st millennium BCE, and Egyptologists reject his revised chronology, which conflicts with astronomical, radiocarbon and documentary evidence. Scholars of mythology also note that his readings of myths were highly selective.

title: The Rigveda is composed
summary: In the Punjab region, priest-poets compose the hymns of the Rigveda, the oldest scripture of Hinduism, passed down orally for centuries.
description: The Rigveda is a collection of 1,028 hymns in Vedic Sanskrit addressed to deities such as Indra, Agni and Soma, composed in the land of seven rivers of the north-western subcontinent by largely pastoral Indo-Aryan-speaking communities. It was transmitted orally with extraordinary precision for many centuries before being written down, and it is the oldest of the four Vedas, the foundational texts of Hinduism. Its language is closely related to that of the Avesta of ancient Iran, and the arrival of Indo-Aryan languages in South Asia is generally linked to migrations from the Central Asian steppe in the 2nd millennium BCE, a view strongly supported by recent genetic studies. Dates for its composition are estimated mainly from linguistic evidence and are approximate.

title: Out of India: 'Indigenous Aryans' theory (fringe claim)
dateLabel: set against the conventional date of the Rigveda, c. 1500 BCE
summary: Proponents claim the Vedic 'Aryans' were native to India, that the Indus cities were Vedic, and that Indo-European languages spread outward from India.
description: The Indigenous Aryans theory, also called Out of India, holds that speakers of Indo-Aryan languages did not migrate into South Asia but had always lived there, and some versions argue that the whole Indo-European language family spread outward from India. Proponents often identify the Indus Valley Civilisation with the society of the Rigveda, date the Vedic hymns to the 4th millennium BCE or earlier, and equate the dried-up Ghaggar-Hakra river with the Sarasvati praised in the Vedas. The idea gained ground from the late 20th century, partly in reaction to colonial-era theories of an 'Aryan invasion' that had been tied to racial hierarchies, and it has been promoted by writers such as Shrikant Talageri, Koenraad Elst and David Frawley. It has wide support in Indian nationalist politics and popular media. The entry is placed at Rakhigarhi, a Harappan city whose ancient DNA has featured prominently in the debate.
mainstreamView: Most linguists, archaeologists and geneticists hold that Indo-Aryan languages arrived in South Asia from the Central Asian steppe during the 2nd millennium BCE, as one strand of the wider Indo-European spread. Ancient-DNA studies since 2018, including a genome from Rakhigarhi published in 2019, show that people of the Indus Valley Civilisation lacked the steppe-related ancestry that entered South Asia after about 2000 BCE and that is found today especially among Indo-European speakers and in traditionally priestly groups. Linguistic evidence points the same way: the language of the Rigveda is very close to Avestan Iranian, its hymns describe horses and spoke-wheeled chariots that are scarcely attested at Indus sites, and the shared vocabulary and branching of the Indo-European family fit a homeland north of the Black and Caspian seas far better than one in India. Scholars stress that these were gradual movements of people who mixed with local populations, not the sudden 'invasion' of colonial-era accounts.

title: Hatshepsut rules Egypt as pharaoh
summary: Hatshepsut, widow of Thutmose II, takes the full titles of pharaoh and sends a celebrated trading expedition to the land of Punt.
description: Hatshepsut first acted as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III and then, within a few years, was crowned king herself, ruling as senior co-pharaoh and often depicted with traditional male regalia, including a false beard. Her reign was prosperous and largely peaceful, marked by building projects such as her terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari. Its reliefs record an expedition by sea to Punt, a region probably on the southern Red Sea coast of Sudan, Eritrea or the Horn of Africa, which brought back myrrh trees, incense, ebony and exotic animals. Late in Thutmose III's reign many of her images and names were erased, possibly to secure his own son's succession rather than out of personal hatred.

title: Olmec civilization arises on the Gulf Coast
summary: At San Lorenzo and later La Venta, in the lowlands of Veracruz and Tabasco, the Olmecs carve colossal stone heads and build Mesoamerica's first major centres.
description: The Olmecs flourished in the tropical lowlands of the southern Gulf of Mexico, first at San Lorenzo (c. 1400–1000 BCE) and later at La Venta (c. 900–400 BCE), where they built earthen platforms and a large clay pyramid. They are best known for colossal basalt heads, probably portraits of rulers, weighing up to about 40 tonnes and hauled from the Tuxtla Mountains, and for finely carved jade. Olmec-style art spread widely across Mesoamerica, and features later shared by the Maya and other peoples, such as the rubber-ball game, ritual bloodletting and possibly early calendrical and writing systems, appear in Olmec contexts. Whether the Olmecs were a 'mother culture' for Mesoamerica or one of several interacting 'sister cultures' is still debated.

title: Dingoes arrive in Australia
summary: Dogs carried by seafarers from Southeast Asia reach Australia and become the dingo, the continent's only dog before European contact.
description: The dingo descends from domestic dogs of East or Southeast Asia that were brought to Australia by people, probably by seafarers from island Southeast Asia. The oldest securely dated dingo remains, from Madura Cave on the Nullarbor Plain, are about 3,350–3,100 years old, although some genetic studies suggest an earlier arrival. Dingoes spread across the mainland but never reached Tasmania, which had been cut off by rising seas, and their arrival may have contributed to the mainland extinction of the thylacine and the Tasmanian devil, alongside climate change and growing human populations. They lived closely with Aboriginal Australians as hunting companions and camp dogs.

title: Akhenaten's religious revolution
summary: Pharaoh Akhenaten elevates the sun-disc Aten above Egypt's other gods and builds a new capital at Amarna, a break later reversed.
description: Amenhotep IV came to the throne around 1353 BCE and soon renamed himself Akhenaten, 'effective for the Aten', promoting the visible disc of the sun as the supreme or only god and neglecting or closing the temples of Amun and other deities. He founded a new capital, Akhetaten, at modern Amarna, where art took on a strikingly informal and elongated style showing the king, Queen Nefertiti and their daughters. Whether his religion was true monotheism or a more limited henotheism is debated. The Amarna letters, a cache of diplomatic correspondence in Akkadian cuneiform found at the site, document Egypt's dealings with Babylon, Mitanni, the Hittites and Canaanite vassals. After his death the old cults were restored under Tutankhamun, and later kings struck Akhenaten from the official record.

title: Lapita voyagers sail into Remote Oceania
summary: Bearers of the Lapita culture spread from the Bismarck Archipelago across thousands of kilometres of open ocean to Vanuatu, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa.
description: The Lapita cultural complex, named after a site in New Caledonia and recognised by its finely dentate-stamped pottery, appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago north-east of New Guinea around 1350 BCE, combining Austronesian seafaring traditions that ultimately originated in Taiwan with local Melanesian elements. Within a few centuries Lapita people sailed in outrigger canoes beyond the Solomon Islands into previously uninhabited Remote Oceania, reaching Vanuatu and New Caledonia by about 1000 BCE and Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 900–800 BCE. Ancient DNA from the Teouma cemetery in Vanuatu shows that these first settlers were of largely East Asian ancestry. They carried pigs, dogs, chickens and crop plants, and their descendants became the ancestral Polynesians who, some two thousand years later, settled the far corners of the Pacific.

title: Reign of Ramesses II
summary: Ramesses II rules Egypt for 66 years, carving colossal temples at Abu Simbel and stamping his name on monuments across the land.
description: Ramesses II, third king of the Nineteenth Dynasty, reigned for about 66 years, probably from 1279 to 1213 BCE, and is often regarded as the most powerful pharaoh of the New Kingdom. He campaigned in the Levant and Nubia, fought the Hittites at Kadesh and later made peace with them, and built a new capital, Pi-Ramesses, in the eastern Delta. His building programme was enormous: the rock-cut temples of Abu Simbel in Nubia, the Ramesseum at Thebes and additions to Karnak and Luxor, often with colossal statues of himself. He fathered dozens of children and outlived many of them. The Abu Simbel temples were cut into blocks and moved to higher ground in the 1960s to save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

title: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Ramesses II and the Hittite king Muwatalli II clash near Kadesh in Syria in what may be the largest chariot battle ever fought.
description: In the fifth year of Ramesses II's reign the Egyptian army marched north to contest control of Syria with the Hittite Empire. Misled by planted informants, Ramesses camped near the city of Kadesh on the Orontes, where a massive Hittite chariot attack routed one of his divisions before reinforcements and the king's own counter-attack restored the situation. With perhaps 5,000–6,000 chariots involved in total, it is among the earliest battles whose tactics and formations are known in detail. Ramesses proclaimed a great victory on temple walls across Egypt, but Hittite records and the aftermath suggest a stalemate, with Kadesh remaining under Hittite influence. Some fifteen years later the two powers concluded the Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty, the oldest known peace treaty whose text survives from both sides.

title: Battle in the Tollense Valley
summary: Bones and weapons from the Tollense Valley in north-east Germany reveal a Bronze Age battle that may have involved thousands of warriors.
description: Since the 1990s, excavations along the Tollense river in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania have recovered the remains of well over 100 individuals, mostly young men, together with bronze and flint arrowheads, wooden clubs and bronze weapons, all dated to around 1250 BCE. Many skeletons bear fresh wounds, including arrowheads lodged in bone, as well as healed injuries from earlier fights, indicating a violent clash at a river crossing. Extrapolating from the excavated area, researchers estimate that perhaps 2,000 or more people took part, some of them apparently from distant regions, as isotope analyses and foreign-style equipment suggest. It is the earliest known large-scale battlefield in northern Europe and challenges the image of the Bronze Age north as a world of small-scale raiding.

title: Oracle bones: earliest known Chinese writing
summary: Diviners of the Shang king at Anyang inscribe questions to the ancestors on turtle shells and ox bones, the oldest substantial Chinese texts.
description: From the reign of King Wu Ding, around 1250 BCE, Shang diviners at the last capital, Yin, recorded questions on prepared turtle plastrons and cattle shoulder blades and then applied heat to produce cracks that were read as answers. Topics included harvests, weather, warfare, childbirth, illness and sacrifices to royal ancestors, and the inscriptions often note the outcome. More than 150,000 fragments have been found since the bones were recognised in 1899, when some sold as 'dragon bones' for traditional medicine were noticed to bear writing. The script, a direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, is already a mature system, and its texts confirmed the list of Shang kings recorded by historians a thousand years later.

title: The Exodus (historicity debated)
summary: The Hebrew Bible tells of Moses leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt to Sinai and Canaan, a founding story whose historicity is debated.
description: The Book of Exodus describes the enslavement of the Israelites in Egypt, the plagues, the crossing of the sea, the giving of the law at Mount Sinai and forty years in the wilderness, events central to Jewish identity and commemorated at Passover. Biblical chronology (1 Kings 6:1) implies a date around 1446 BCE, while the mention of the store city of Ramesses has led many to prefer the 13th century BCE, in the reign of Ramesses II. No Egyptian record mentions the event, and surveys of Sinai have found no trace of a large migrating population in that period. The story was probably shaped over centuries and reached its present written form during or after the Babylonian exile.
mainstreamView: Most archaeologists and biblical scholars conclude that the Exodus as described, with 600,000 men and their families, did not happen, and that the early Israelites emerged largely from the indigenous population of Canaan. Many think the story may preserve memories of smaller groups who left Egypt, of Semitic people living in Egypt such as the Hyksos, or of Egyptian rule over Canaan, while some scholars still argue for a more substantial historical core.

title: Zoroaster and the Gathas
summary: The Iranian prophet Zarathustra composes the Gathas, hymns that found Zoroastrianism around a supreme wise god, Ahura Mazda.
description: Zoroaster (Zarathustra) was a priest and poet of the eastern Iranian world whose Gathas, seventeen hymns preserved in the Avesta, proclaim Ahura Mazda as the wise creator and frame existence as a struggle between truth (asha) and the lie (druj). The religion that grew from his teaching became the faith of successive Persian empires, and many scholars think its ideas of a final judgement, heaven and hell, and a coming saviour influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam. His date is uncertain: the archaic language of the Gathas, very close to that of the Rigveda, and the pastoral society they describe lead many scholars to place him between about 1500 and 1000 BCE, while a later tradition places him in the 7th or 6th century BCE. His homeland is usually located in Central Asia or eastern Iran.
mainstreamView: Zoroaster's historicity is broadly accepted on the basis of the Gathas, but his dates are genuinely disputed: linguistic evidence favours the late 2nd millennium BCE, while the traditional date of '258 years before Alexander' points to the 6th century BCE. This entry uses a representative date of about 1200 BCE.

title: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within a few decades the Hittite Empire, the Mycenaean palaces, Ugarit and other states of the eastern Mediterranean are destroyed or abandoned.
description: Around 1200 BCE the interconnected palace societies of the eastern Mediterranean fell apart. Hattusa was abandoned and the Hittite Empire disintegrated, Mycenaean palaces such as Pylos burned and Linear B writing disappeared, and cities including Ugarit on the Syrian coast were destroyed, its last letters warning of enemy ships. Egypt survived but was weakened, and Babylonia and Assyria contracted. Proposed causes include prolonged drought recorded in pollen and lake sediments, earthquakes, famine, internal revolts, the breakdown of long-distance trade in copper and tin, and raiders including the 'Sea Peoples'. Most historians now see a systems collapse in which several of these stresses reinforced one another. In the aftermath came a centuries-long 'dark age' in Greece, but also the rise of new players such as the Phoenicians, Israelites, Arameans and Philistines, and the spread of iron.

title: The Iron Age begins
summary: After the Bronze Age collapse, smelted iron tools and weapons spread across the eastern Mediterranean and Near East, gradually replacing bronze.
description: Iron had long been known, at first from meteorites, as in a dagger buried with Tutankhamun, and smelted iron was produced in small quantities in Anatolia during the 2nd millennium BCE, though the old idea of a secret Hittite monopoly is now doubted. After about 1200 BCE, perhaps partly because disrupted trade made the tin needed for bronze scarce, smiths in Cyprus, the Levant and Anatolia began producing iron on a larger scale, and carburised, quenched iron, an early form of steel, proved harder than bronze. Because iron ore is far more widespread than copper and tin, the metal eventually made tools and weapons cheaper and more widely available. Ironworking spread across the Near East, the Aegean and northern India by about 1000 BCE and into central Europe a few centuries later, while iron smelting in sub-Saharan Africa, attested from the 1st millennium BCE, may have arisen independently. The start of the Iron Age varies by region and is a conventional label rather than a single event.

title: Ramesses III repels the Sea Peoples
summary: In his eighth year, Ramesses III defeats a coalition of migrating 'Sea Peoples' on land and in a naval battle at the mouths of the Nile.
description: Inscriptions and reliefs on Ramesses III's mortuary temple at Medinet Habu describe a confederation of peoples, including the Peleset, Tjeker, Shekelesh, Denyen and Weshesh, who had overrun Hatti, Cyprus and the Syrian coast and then advanced on Egypt with warships and with ox-carts carrying their families. The pharaoh claims to have crushed them in a land battle on the Levantine frontier and in a naval engagement in the Nile Delta, one of the earliest sea battles depicted in art. The Peleset are widely identified with the biblical Philistines, who settled on the southern coast of Canaan soon afterwards. The origins of the Sea Peoples, possibly in the Aegean, western Anatolia or the central Mediterranean, and their role in the wider Bronze Age collapse are still debated.

title: The Phoenician alphabet
summary: Phoenician scribes standardise a 22-letter consonantal alphabet that becomes the ancestor of the Greek, Latin, Hebrew, Arabic and many other scripts.
description: The Phoenician alphabet developed from the earlier Proto-Sinaitic and Proto-Canaanite scripts, which adapted Egyptian hieroglyphic signs to write a Semitic language during the 2nd millennium BCE. By around 1050 BCE the Phoenician city-states of Byblos, Tyre and Sidon were using a standardised set of 22 letters for consonants, written right to left; one of the earliest long inscriptions is on the sarcophagus of King Ahiram of Byblos. Because it needed only a couple of dozen signs, the alphabet was far easier to learn than cuneiform or hieroglyphs. Phoenician traders carried it around the Mediterranean, and it was adapted into the Aramaic, Hebrew and Greek alphabets, from which Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic and, probably via Aramaic, the Brahmic scripts of India descend.

title: Zhou conquest and the Mandate of Heaven
summary: King Wu of Zhou defeats the last Shang king at Muye and founds China's longest-lasting dynasty, justified by the 'Mandate of Heaven'.
description: According to traditional accounts the Zhou, a people from the Wei River valley in the west, defeated the Shang at the Battle of Muye, near the Shang capital, after which the last Shang king killed himself. The date of 1046 BCE adopted by the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project is widely used, though other estimates range from 1122 to 1018 BCE. To legitimise the conquest the Zhou rulers, especially the Duke of Zhou, developed the idea of the Mandate of Heaven: Heaven grants the right to rule to a virtuous dynasty and withdraws it from a corrupt one. This principle was used to justify the rise and fall of Chinese dynasties for three thousand years. The Western Zhou ruled from capitals near modern Xi'an through a network of kin-based vassal states until 771 BCE, and the dynasty lasted nominally until 256 BCE.

title: David, Solomon and the kingdoms of Israel and Judah
summary: The Bible describes a united kingdom under David and Solomon centred on Jerusalem; how large and powerful it really was is debated.
description: According to the books of Samuel and Kings, David captured Jerusalem around 1000 BCE and made it the capital of a united kingdom of Israel, and his son Solomon built the First Temple before the realm split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south around 930 BCE. Outside the Bible, the 9th-century BCE Tel Dan stele refers to the 'House of David', indicating that a royal dynasty traced its descent from a founder named David. Archaeological evidence for a large 10th-century state is limited and contested, and some scholars argue that the northern kingdom of Israel, ruled from Samaria by the Omride dynasty in the 9th century, was the first substantial Israelite state. Israel was conquered by Assyria in 722–720 BCE, while Judah survived until the Babylonian conquest of 587/586 BCE.
mainstreamView: Most scholars accept that David was a historical ruler, since the Tel Dan inscription names a 'House of David', and many also accept Solomon, although no inscription from his reign has been found. They disagree on whether these kings governed a powerful, centralised kingdom or a modest highland chiefdom, and disputes over the dating of excavated strata (the 'low chronology') are central to the disagreement.

title: Aguada Fénix: oldest known Maya monument
summary: Early Maya communities build a vast earthen platform 1.4 km long in Tabasco, Mexico, centuries before the rise of Maya kings.
description: Aguada Fénix, revealed by airborne lidar survey and announced in 2020, is a raised rectangular platform about 1,400 m long, 400 m wide and 10–15 m high, built around 1000–800 BCE; it is the oldest and largest known monumental construction in the Maya region. Unlike later Maya cities it has no palaces, royal tombs or clear signs of strong social inequality, suggesting that early communities, some perhaps still partly mobile, cooperated in large communal projects before the emergence of kings. Together with Ceibal in Guatemala, where a ceremonial complex dates to about 1000 BCE, it shows that Maya civilization developed in interaction with the Olmec world rather than simply deriving from it.

title: Rohl's New Chronology of Egypt (fringe claim)
dateLabel: c. 925 BCE (Shishak; Rohl places Ramesses II in the 10th century BCE)
summary: British author David Rohl argues that Egyptian dates should be lowered by up to 350 years, making Ramesses II the biblical Shishak who plundered Jerusalem.
description: In A Test of Time (1995) and later books, David Rohl argued that the conventional chronology of ancient Egypt is too long, chiefly because the dynasties of the Third Intermediate Period overlapped far more than Egyptologists allow. Lowering New Kingdom and earlier dates by up to about 350 years would, in his scheme, place Ramesses II in the 10th century BCE and make him Shishak, the pharaoh who in the Bible plunders Jerusalem around 925 BCE, while Joseph, the Exodus and the conquest of Canaan would fall in the Middle Kingdom and Second Intermediate Period, where Rohl claims to find archaeological traces of them. He also proposed that the Amarna letters of Akhenaten's reign describe the time of Saul and David. His ideas reached a wide audience through a 1995 British television series and belong to a wider family of revised chronologies, including Peter James's Centuries of Darkness (1991). They are unrelated to Anatoly Fomenko's far more radical 'New Chronology'. The entry is placed at Karnak, where the conventional Shishak, Sheshonq I, recorded his campaign.
mainstreamView: Egyptologists reject the New Chronology. Radiocarbon dates on short-lived plant remains from securely dated Egyptian contexts, published in a large 2010 study, fit the conventional chronology to within a few decades and rule out a shift of centuries. Synchronisms with Assyria and Babylonia, whose chronologies are anchored by records such as the eclipse of 763 BCE, tie Egyptian reigns to an independent framework. Most scholars identify the biblical Shishak with Sheshonq I of the 22nd Dynasty, whose campaign into Canaan is listed on the Bubastite Portal at Karnak, and Rohl's proposed archaeological matches for Joseph and the Exodus have not been accepted.

title: The Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: From Assur, Nimrud and Nineveh, Assyrian kings build the largest empire yet seen, ruling from Egypt to western Iran with a professional army.
description: Beginning with Adad-nirari II in 911 BCE, Assyria's kings reconquered lost lands and, from the reign of Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727 BCE), built a centralised empire of provinces with a standing army, iron weapons, siege engines and a fast royal messenger system. Mass deportation of conquered populations, including the northern Israelites, was deliberate policy. Under Sennacherib, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal the empire reached Egypt, Anatolia and Elam, palaces at Nimrud, Khorsabad and Nineveh were lined with carved reliefs of war and hunting, and Ashurbanipal assembled a great library of cuneiform tablets. Overstretched by civil war, the empire fell to a coalition of Babylonians and Medes, who sacked Nineveh in 612 BCE; the last Assyrian forces were defeated at Harran in 609 BCE.

title: Cascajal Block: the oldest writing in the Americas?
summary: A serpentine slab from Veracruz bears 62 signs that some scholars hail as Olmec writing from about 900 BCE, the earliest in the Americas.
description: The Cascajal Block was found by road builders in a gravel quarry in the Olmec heartland of Veracruz, Mexico, and published by a team of archaeologists in 2006. Its flat face carries 62 incised signs, some repeated in sequences, which the authors argued represent a true writing system dating from the San Lorenzo phase, around 900 BCE, centuries before the earliest known Zapotec and Maya inscriptions. The text has not been deciphered. Its discoverers stressed that the signs follow consistent patterns and include motifs known from Olmec art.
mainstreamView: Many Mesoamericanists accept the block as authentic and possibly early writing, but because it was found out of its original archaeological context its date rests on pottery recovered from the same quarry debris; some critics question whether it records language at all, and no comparable Olmec texts have been found.

title: Chavín de Huántar and the Chavín cult
summary: A temple complex high in the Peruvian Andes becomes a pilgrimage centre whose feline and serpent imagery spreads across much of Peru.
description: Chavín de Huántar, at about 3,150 m in the Andes of north-central Peru, grew from around 900 BCE, with some earlier construction, into a ceremonial centre of stone platforms, sunken plazas and labyrinthine underground galleries. At its heart stands the Lanzón, a carved granite shaft about 4.5 m tall depicting a fanged deity. Excavations suggest that priests used acoustics, water channels, light and psychoactive substances such as the San Pedro cactus to create powerful ritual experiences. Chavín art, featuring jaguars, caimans, serpents and raptors, spread widely across the coast and highlands, suggesting a shared religious ideology and making it one of the earliest unifying cultural horizons in the Andes.

title: Nok terracottas and early West African iron
summary: In central Nigeria the Nok culture creates sub-Saharan Africa's oldest known large figurative sculptures and smelts some of West Africa's earliest iron.
description: The Nok culture, named after the village in central Nigeria where tin miners found the first terracotta in 1928, is known for large, hollow fired-clay sculptures of human figures with elaborately styled hair and distinctive triangular or D-shaped eyes. Long-term research indicates that Nok farming communities appeared around 1500 BCE and that the sculptures were made from about 900 BCE until around the turn of the era. Furnaces at Nok sites show iron smelting by the mid-1st millennium BCE, among the earliest in West Africa; whether sub-Saharan iron metallurgy was invented locally or introduced from North Africa is still debated. Looting for the international art market has destroyed many sites and hampered research.

title: Phoenicians found Carthage
dateLabel: 814 BCE (traditional); earliest remains late 9th–8th century BCE
summary: Settlers from Tyre found Carthage on the coast of North Africa, a trading colony that grows into a Mediterranean power.
description: Phoenician merchants from Tyre and Sidon established trading posts across the Mediterranean, from Cyprus and Sicily to Sardinia, North Africa and Gadir (Cádiz) beyond the Strait of Gibraltar, seeking silver, tin and markets for their purple dye, glass and crafted goods. Carthage, whose name means 'new city', was by Greek tradition founded in 814 BCE by Elissa (Dido), a princess fleeing Tyre; pottery from the earliest excavated levels was long dated to the mid-8th century BCE, but radiocarbon dates on animal bones from those levels suggest the late 9th century, close to the traditional date. Its sheltered harbour and position near the narrowest point of the Mediterranean made it a commercial hub. Carthage later led the western Phoenician colonies and became Rome's great rival until its destruction in 146 BCE.

title: Scythian horse nomads of the steppe
summary: Mounted nomads of the Eurasian steppe, known to the Greeks as Scythians, build rich royal burial mounds from Siberia to the Black Sea.
description: From about the 9th century BCE a way of life based on mounted pastoralism spread across the Eurasian steppe, from southern Siberia and Mongolia to the lands north of the Black Sea. One of the earliest known Scythian-type royal burials, the Arzhan-1 kurgan in Tuva, dates to around 800 BCE and already contains mass horse sacrifices and early 'animal style' art. In the 7th century BCE Scythian warriors raided through the Caucasus into the Near East, and the Greek historian Herodotus later described their customs in detail. Expert mounted archers, they controlled routes linking China, Iran and the Greek world, and their elites were buried with spectacular gold work.

title: Hallstatt culture and Iron Age Europe
summary: Iron Age communities in central Europe grow rich from salt mining at Hallstatt in Austria and from trade with the Mediterranean world.
description: The Hallstatt culture, named after a cemetery of more than a thousand graves above a salt mine in the Austrian Alps, was the dominant early Iron Age culture of central Europe from about 800 to 450 BCE. Salt, essential for preserving food, was mined deep inside the mountain, where wooden tools, textiles and even a Bronze Age wooden staircase have survived in the salty conditions. Elites from eastern France to Slovenia were buried with wagons, weapons and imported Greek and Etruscan luxuries, as in the princely graves of Hochdorf and Vix. Many scholars associate the Hallstatt and succeeding La Tène cultures with early Celtic-speaking peoples, though linking archaeological cultures to languages is debated.

title: Olmec origins from Africa or China (fringe claim)
dateLabel: c. 800–700 BCE (date proposed by Van Sertima)
summary: Some writers claim that the Olmec colossal heads depict Africans, or that refugees from Shang China founded Olmec civilization.
description: Since the 19th century, observers have speculated about Olmec origins on the basis of the broad noses and full lips of the colossal stone heads. Ivan Van Sertima's They Came Before Columbus (1976) argued that Nubian and Egyptian voyagers reached the Gulf Coast around 800–700 BCE, during Kush's 25th Dynasty, and shaped Olmec culture, while others, including the archaeologist Betty Meggers in 1975, proposed that people fleeing the fall of the Shang dynasty around 1100 BCE crossed the Pacific and inspired Olmec art and writing. Such ideas remain popular in some publications and online.
mainstreamView: Archaeologists trace Olmec culture to earlier local developments on the Gulf Coast, with farming, pottery and settlement sequences that predate any proposed contact; Olmec civilization was already flourishing at San Lorenzo by 1400–1200 BCE, before either supposed arrival. No African or Chinese artefacts, crops, scripts, diseases or genetic signatures have been found in Olmec contexts, genetic studies of ancient and modern Mesoamericans show no sign of such contact, and the facial features of the heads fall within the normal range of Indigenous people of the region. Scholars note that these theories, however well-intentioned, deny Indigenous Mesoamericans credit for their own achievements.

title: The early Upanishads
summary: In the Ganges valley, Vedic thinkers compose the earliest Upanishads, teaching that the self (atman) is one with ultimate reality (brahman).
description: The Upanishads are philosophical texts that form the concluding portion of the Vedas. The oldest, such as the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya Upanishads, were composed largely as prose dialogues, often featuring sages such as Yajnavalkya at the courts of kings like Janaka of Videha in the eastern Ganges plain. They shift attention from ritual sacrifice to inner knowledge and explore concepts that became central to Indian religion, including atman, brahman, karma, rebirth (samsara) and liberation (moksha). These ideas, developed alongside movements of wandering ascetics, deeply influenced Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism. Their dates are estimated from linguistic and textual evidence and are approximate.

title: First recorded Olympic Games
summary: At the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia, the first Olympic Games are traditionally held, with a single footrace won by Koroibos of Elis.
description: Greek tradition dated the first Olympiad to 776 BCE, a date worked out around 400 BCE by the sophist Hippias of Elis from lists of victors and later used by Greek historians to count years. The earliest recorded event was the stadion, a sprint of about 192 m, said to have been won by a cook named Koroibos. Over time the festival, held every four years in honour of Zeus, added longer races, wrestling, boxing, the pentathlon and chariot racing, and a sacred truce allowed athletes and spectators to travel safely. Archaeological evidence suggests that cult activity at the sanctuary is older than 776 BCE and that the traditional date is approximate. The ancient Games continued for more than a thousand years, until the late 4th century CE.

title: Founding of Rome (legendary date)
summary: According to Roman legend, Romulus founds Rome on the Palatine Hill on 21 April 753 BCE after killing his twin brother Remus.
description: Roman tradition held that the city was founded by Romulus, a son of the god Mars who was raised with his twin Remus by a she-wolf, and the scholar Varro's calculation of 753 BCE became the standard starting point for counting years ab urbe condita. Archaeology shows that the Palatine and neighbouring hills were occupied by Iron Age villages from around 1000 BCE, which gradually merged into a city during the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, with the Forum valley drained and paved by about 600 BCE. Under its kings, some of them Etruscan, Rome became a significant city of Latium. From these modest beginnings grew a state that would come to dominate the Mediterranean world.

title: Homer's Iliad and Odyssey
summary: The Iliad and the Odyssey, epics attributed to Homer, take shape in Ionia and become the foundation of Greek literature and education.
description: The Iliad, about the wrath of Achilles during the Trojan War, and the Odyssey, about Odysseus's long voyage home, grew out of a centuries-old tradition of orally composed poetry in dactylic hexameter. Most scholars date their composition to the late 8th or 7th century BCE, around the time the Greeks adopted the Phoenician alphabet and added letters for vowels, which made it possible to write the poems down. Whether 'Homer' was a single poet, two poets or a name for a tradition is the long-running 'Homeric Question'; ancient tradition placed him in Ionia, on the coast of Asia Minor or on the island of Chios. The poems shaped Greek religion, values and education and remain among the most influential works of world literature.

title: Greek colonisation of the Mediterranean
summary: Greek city-states found hundreds of colonies, from Marseille and southern Italy to the Black Sea and Libya, spreading Greek culture widely.
description: From the 8th century BCE, pressure on land, trade and political strife led Greek cities such as Corinth, Chalcis, Miletus and Megara to send out groups of settlers to found independent new cities (apoikiai). Pithekoussai on Ischia was established around 770 BCE, followed by Syracuse (traditionally 734/733 BCE) and many other cities of Sicily and southern Italy, later known as Magna Graecia, as well as Byzantium, Cyrene in Libya and Massalia (Marseille) around 600 BCE. Miletus alone was credited with dozens of colonies around the Black Sea. The colonies spread the Greek alphabet, coinage, wine and olive cultivation, and architecture across the Mediterranean, and brought Greeks into close contact with Etruscans, Phoenicians, Scythians and Celts.

title: Kushite pharaohs rule Egypt
summary: Kings of Kush from Napata in Sudan conquer Egypt and rule as the 25th Dynasty, reviving ancient traditions and pyramid building.
description: The kingdom of Kush, centred on Napata near the sacred mountain of Jebel Barkal in modern Sudan, grew strong after Egyptian control of Nubia ended. Around 727 BCE King Piye marched north and subdued the rival rulers of a fragmented Egypt, and his successors Shabaka, Shebitku and Taharqa ruled the whole Nile valley from the Delta to beyond the Fourth Cataract as the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. They restored temples, revived Old Kingdom artistic styles and were buried under steep pyramids at el-Kurru and Nuri. Assyrian invasions of Egypt in 671 and 664–663 BCE forced them back to Nubia, where the kingdom of Kush continued for roughly another thousand years, later centred on Meroë.

title: The first coins in Lydia
summary: In the kingdom of Lydia, in western Anatolia, lumps of electrum stamped with a lion's head become the world's first coins.
description: The earliest known coins were made of electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver found in the river Pactolus at the Lydian capital Sardis, and were stamped with designs such as a lion's head to guarantee their weight. Finds from a foundation deposit of the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus help date the first issues to roughly 630–600 BCE, under the Lydian kings, perhaps Alyattes. Around 550 BCE King Croesus, whose wealth became proverbial, is credited with introducing separate coins of pure gold and silver. Coinage spread rapidly to the Greek cities of Ionia and the mainland, while in China bronze spade- and knife-shaped money developed separately. Coins transformed trade, taxation and the payment of soldiers.

title: Phoenicians sail around Africa?
summary: Herodotus reports that Phoenician sailors sent by Pharaoh Necho II sailed around Africa from the Red Sea in about three years.
description: In his Histories, Herodotus records that Necho II, who ruled Egypt from 610 to 595 BCE, sent Phoenician crews south from the Red Sea with orders to return through the Pillars of Heracles, the Strait of Gibraltar. According to the story they sailed for more than two years, landing each autumn to sow and harvest grain, and returned to Egypt in the third year. Herodotus himself doubted one detail: the sailors claimed that, while rounding the southern end of Libya, they had the sun on their right, that is, to the north. That is exactly what would be observed south of the equator, and the detail is often cited as evidence that the voyage really took place.
mainstreamView: Many historians consider the voyage plausible and see the sun observation as a strong argument in its favour, but there is no independent evidence or archaeological trace, and some scholars regard the account as a traveller's tale; the first verified rounding of southern Africa was by Bartolomeu Dias in 1488 CE.

title: Mahavira and Jainism
summary: Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th Jain tirthankara, renounces princely life and teaches strict non-violence, asceticism and the many-sidedness of truth.
description: Mahavira was born into a ruling family near Vaishali in the eastern Ganges plain, in modern Bihar, and according to tradition renounced his position at about 30 to become a wandering ascetic. After more than twelve years of austerities he attained kevala jnana, omniscient knowledge, and taught for some three decades. Jains regard him as the 24th and last tirthankara of the present cosmic age, renewing a tradition associated with his predecessor Parshvanatha, and his teachings emphasise ahimsa (non-violence toward all living beings), truthfulness, non-attachment and anekantavada, the many-sidedness of truth. The traditional dates of 599–527 BCE are widely used, but many historians prefer a later chronology, with his death around 468 BCE or later, making him a contemporary of the Buddha.

title: Solon's reforms in Athens
summary: The Athenian statesman Solon cancels debts, ends debt slavery and ties political rights to wealth rather than birth.
description: Chosen as archon in 594 BCE, or shortly afterwards, amid a crisis between wealthy landowners and indebted peasants, Solon introduced the seisachtheia, the 'shaking-off of burdens', which cancelled debts secured on land and persons and freed Athenians enslaved for debt. He replaced most of Draco's harsh laws, divided citizens into four classes by agricultural income to determine eligibility for office, and gave all citizens access to the assembly and to popular courts. He also wrote poems defending his reforms, some of which survive. Although a tyranny under Peisistratus followed, Solon's laws laid foundations on which Athenian democracy was later built.

title: Fall of Jerusalem and the Babylonian exile
summary: Nebuchadnezzar II destroys Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple and deports much of Judah's elite to Babylon, transforming Jewish religion.
description: After Judah rebelled against Babylonian rule, Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem, deporting King Jehoiachin and many leading citizens in 597 BCE and then destroying the city and its Temple in 587 or 586 BCE. Babylonian ration tablets naming Jehoiachin and records of Judean settlements near Babylon confirm parts of the biblical account. In exile the Judean community preserved its identity around the Torah, Sabbath observance and circumcision, and much of the Hebrew Bible was compiled or edited in this period. After Cyrus the Great conquered Babylon in 539 BCE, exiles were permitted to return, and the Second Temple was completed around 516 BCE.

title: Thales and the first Greek philosophy
summary: Thales of Miletus, said to have predicted the solar eclipse of 28 May 585 BCE, seeks natural rather than mythical explanations for the world.
description: Thales of Miletus, a city on the Ionian coast of Asia Minor, was regarded by Aristotle and later tradition as the first Greek philosopher. He proposed that water is the underlying substance of all things, an attempt to explain nature without appealing to the gods, and was credited with geometric theorems and practical knowledge drawn partly from Egypt and Babylon. According to Herodotus he foretold the year of a solar eclipse that halted a battle between the Lydians and the Medes, usually identified with the eclipse of 28 May 585 BCE. Whether he could really have predicted it is debated, but his successors Anaximander and Anaximenes continued the Milesian search for rational explanations, the beginning of Western natural philosophy and science.

title: Laozi and the Tao Te Ching
summary: Tradition names Laozi, an archivist at the Zhou court, as the author of the Tao Te Ching, the founding text of Daoism.
