description: According to Sima Qian's biography, written in the 1st century BCE, Laozi ('Old Master') was a keeper of archives at the Zhou court who was consulted by Confucius and wrote the Tao Te Ching before departing westward. The short book teaches that the Dao, the ineffable 'Way' underlying all things, is best followed through simplicity, spontaneity and non-coercive action (wu wei), and it became the central text of philosophical and religious Daoism. Already in Sima Qian's time accounts of Laozi were uncertain, and many modern scholars doubt that he was a single historical person. Bamboo manuscripts excavated at Guodian, dating to around 300 BCE, contain the earliest known versions of parts of the text.
mainstreamView: Most modern scholars regard the Tao Te Ching as a compilation that reached its familiar form in the 4th or 3rd century BCE, drawing on earlier sayings; whether a historical Laozi lived in the 6th century BCE cannot be confirmed, and some regard him as a legendary figure.

title: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha
dateLabel: traditionally c. 563–483 BCE (many scholars: c. 480–400 BCE)
summary: Siddhartha Gautama of the Shakya clan renounces home life, attains awakening at Bodh Gaya and founds Buddhism, which later spreads across Asia.
description: Siddhartha Gautama was born into the Shakya clan at Lumbini, in what is now southern Nepal. According to Buddhist tradition he left his family at 29 to seek release from suffering, tried and rejected extreme asceticism, and attained awakening while meditating beneath a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya. He gave his first sermon at Sarnath, near Varanasi, teaching the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path as a middle way, and spent some 45 years teaching across the Ganges plain and founding a monastic order before dying at Kushinagar at about 80. His dates are uncertain: the traditional chronology places his life around 563–483 BCE, but many scholars now favour a death date around 400 BCE. Buddhism went on to spread through South, Central, East and Southeast Asia and today has several hundred million followers.

title: Confucius
summary: Confucius, a scholar and minor official in the state of Lu, teaches an ethics of virtue, ritual and family duty that will shape East Asia.
description: Kong Qiu, known as Kongzi or Confucius, was born in the state of Lu in eastern China during the turbulent Spring and Autumn period, when the authority of the Zhou kings had declined. After a modest career in government and years travelling among rival courts in search of a ruler who would adopt his ideas, he devoted himself to teaching. He emphasised ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety), filial piety and government by moral example, and looked back to the early Zhou as a model of good order. His sayings were compiled by his disciples in the Analects, and Confucianism later became the official ideology of the Han dynasty and the foundation of education, government and family life in China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for more than two thousand years.

title: Cyrus the Great founds the Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus II of Persia overthrows the Medes, then conquers Lydia and Babylon, creating the largest empire the world had yet seen.
description: Cyrus II, king of Anshan in southwestern Iran, defeated his overlord Astyages of Media around 550 BCE, conquered Croesus's Lydia around 547 BCE and took Babylon in 539 BCE, uniting most of the Near East under Persian rule. Building his capital at Pasargadae, he won a reputation among Greeks and Jews alike for tolerating the customs and religions of conquered peoples. Under his successors Cambyses II, who added Egypt, and Darius I, the Achaemenid Empire stretched from the Balkans and Libya to the Indus valley, the largest empire the world had yet seen. It endured until its conquest by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE.

title: Cyrus takes Babylon: the Cyrus Cylinder
summary: Cyrus captures Babylon almost without a fight and issues a clay cylinder presenting himself as a restorer of temples and displaced peoples.
description: In October 539 BCE Persian forces defeated the Babylonian army at Opis and entered Babylon, ending the Neo-Babylonian Empire of Nabonidus. Soon afterwards a barrel-shaped clay cylinder inscribed in Akkadian cuneiform was buried in the city's foundations, presenting Cyrus as chosen by the god Marduk to replace an impious king and describing how he returned gods' images and displaced peoples to their homes. Found in 1879 and now in the British Museum, it has been called the first charter of human rights, notably by the last Shah of Iran, but most historians see it as conventional Mesopotamian royal propaganda. Its policy is nonetheless consistent with the biblical account of Cyrus allowing the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem.

title: Pythagoras founds his school at Croton
summary: Pythagoras of Samos settles in Croton in southern Italy and founds a community devoted to mathematics, music and a mystical way of life.
description: Pythagoras left Samos around 530 BCE and established a community at Croton in Magna Graecia whose members followed strict rules, believed in the transmigration of souls and held that numbers underlie the order of the cosmos. The Pythagoreans are credited with discovering the numerical ratios behind musical harmonies and with early work in arithmetic and geometry, though Pythagoras's own contributions are hard to separate from those of later followers because he wrote nothing. The theorem that bears his name was known more than a thousand years earlier in Babylon, as shown by the tablet Plimpton 322 of about 1800 BCE, and the Greeks may have been the first to prove it in general form. Pythagorean ideas strongly influenced Plato and later Western thought.

title: Darius I and the Behistun inscription
summary: Darius I seizes the Persian throne, reorganises the empire into satrapies and records his victories on a cliff at Behistun in three languages.
description: Darius I took power in 522 BCE after killing Gaumata, whom he claimed was an impostor posing as Cyrus's son Bardiya, a story many historians treat with caution, and then crushed a wave of revolts across the empire. He commemorated these events in the Behistun inscription, carved high on a cliff in western Iran in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian cuneiform, which became the key to deciphering cuneiform in the 19th century, much as the Rosetta Stone did for hieroglyphs. Darius organised the empire into satrapies paying regular tribute, introduced the gold daric coin, built the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa and began the ceremonial capital of Persepolis. His expedition against Athens ended in defeat at Marathon in 490 BCE.

title: Cleisthenes establishes Athenian democracy
summary: Cleisthenes reorganises Athenian citizens into ten new tribes and gives power to the assembly, laying the foundations of democracy.
description: After the fall of the tyrant Hippias in 510 BCE and a power struggle with the aristocrat Isagoras, who called in Spartan help, Cleisthenes won popular backing and in 508/507 BCE pushed through sweeping reforms. He divided the citizen body into ten tribes, each mixing demes (local districts) from the city, the coast and the inland, to break the power of old aristocratic clans, and created a Council of 500, fifty from each tribe, to prepare business for the citizens' assembly. Ostracism, a vote to exile a dangerous politician for ten years, is also attributed to him. The Athenians later called this system demokratia, 'rule by the people', although women, slaves and foreigners were excluded. It became the model and namesake for later democracies.
